# Fever in children

Notes from our pediatrician's handout, kept with the thermometer. A fever is the body fighting an infection; the number matters less than the child's age and how they act.

## What counts as a fever

A temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher is a fever. A rectal reading is the most accurate for babies; ear and forehead thermometers are fine for older children. An armpit reading runs about a degree low, so a "99.5" there may be a real fever.

## Babies younger than 3 months

Any fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher in a baby under 3 months old is an emergency. Call the pediatrician or go to the emergency department right away, at any hour. Do not give fever medicine first and do not wait to see whether it passes: the doctor needs to see the baby before anything hides the fever.

## Babies and toddlers from 3 months to 3 years

A fever alone is usually not an emergency at this age. Call the pediatrician's office if the temperature is 102°F (38.9°C) or higher, if the fever has lasted more than 24 hours in a child under 2 (or more than 3 days in an older child), or if the child is unusually sleepy, will not drink, or has had no wet diaper in 8 hours. Call 911 for a stiff neck, trouble breathing, or a rash that does not fade when pressed.

## Keeping a feverish child comfortable

Dress them in light clothing, offer small sips of fluid often, and let them rest. A lukewarm sponge bath is fine; cold baths, ice and alcohol rubs are not, because shivering raises the body's temperature. Fever medicine is for comfort, not for bringing the number down to normal.

## Fever seizures

Some children between 6 months and 5 years have a short seizure when a fever climbs fast. Lay the child on their side on a soft surface, loosen clothing, and time it. Most last under 5 minutes and cause no harm. Call 911 if it lasts 5 minutes or longer or the child is hard to wake afterward; call the doctor the same day even if it stops quickly.
